# ARIVA Script: One Effective Exam Prep Strategy

**Generated by:** Skill 03 — Script Generation
**Workshop slug:** exam_prep_strategy
**Duration:** 10 minutes
**Format:** In-person
**Audience:** University students preparing for exams
**ILO:** By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to use retrieval practice as a study method by recalling course content from memory without looking at notes, and identifying gaps to guide further study.

---

## Agenda at a Glance

| Phase | Name | Time | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Arrival | 0:00–1:00 | Name, topic, ILO |
| R | Reactivating | 1:00–2:30 | Show of hands — studied hard, still blanked |
| I | Informing | 2:30–7:00 | The "illusion of knowing" + retrieval practice explained |
| V | Verarbeitung | 7:00–9:30 | Solo recall attempt with own material |
| A | Assessing | 9:30–10:00 | Hands up if you found a gap |

---

## Full Script

---

### A — Arrival [0:00–1:00]

**Purpose:** Orient participants. Name the topic and the ILO. Nothing else — no backstory, no agenda.

> **Script:**
> "Hi, I'm [name]. In the next 10 minutes, you're going to use the most effective study technique most students never use — and by the end, you'll have already done it once. Let's go."

> **Cue:** The ILO is embedded in the Arrival as a promise, not a formal statement. It names an action ("you'll have already done it") and creates mild curiosity. Don't explain what it is yet — let the R phase surface the need first.

**Transition:** Move directly into the reactivation question. No pause.

---

### R — Reactivating [1:00–2:30]

**Purpose:** Surface the problem that retrieval practice solves. Almost every student has experienced studying hard and still blanking — this question creates instant common ground and opens the door.

> **Script:**
> "Quick question before we get into it. Raise your hand if this has ever happened to you: you studied — actually put in real hours — and then sat in the exam and your mind just went blank on something you'd reviewed."
>
> *(Wait. Nearly all hands should go up.)*
>
> "Good. Almost everyone. That experience has a name and, more importantly, a fix. That's what the next 10 minutes are about."

> **Cue:** Look around the room when hands go up. Acknowledge the breadth: "Yeah — most of you." If only a few hands go up, say: "Even if it's only happened once, it's worth knowing why." Don't lose time on it.

**Watch for:** Students who look confused or don't raise their hand — they may be very early in their studies. That's fine; the session is still useful as prevention.

**Transition:** "Here's what's actually happening when that occurs — and what you can do about it."

---

### I — Informing [2:30–7:00]

**Purpose:** Explain the "illusion of knowing" (why re-reading fails) and then introduce retrieval practice as the concrete alternative. Use examples from students' own lives, not academic citations.

**The concept (spine of this phase):**
> Re-reading creates familiarity, not memory. Only active recall — forcing your brain to retrieve without looking — builds the memory trace that survives an exam.

> **Script:**
> "Here's what happens when you re-read your notes. Everything looks familiar. You think: 'Yes, I know this.' But here's the thing — familiar is not the same as remembered. Familiar just means you've seen it before.
>
> The moment you close your notes and try to recall something from scratch — no prompts, no text in front of you — that familiar feeling evaporates. Because recognition and recall are not the same skill. And exams test recall.
>
> There's a good analogy here. Imagine you want to get stronger at push-ups. You could watch videos of other people doing push-ups. You'd recognise exactly what the movement looks like. But you wouldn't get stronger. You need to do the reps yourself. Re-reading is watching the video. Retrieval practice is doing the reps.
>
> So what does retrieval practice actually look like? It's simple: you close your notes, you grab a blank sheet of paper, and you write down everything you can remember about a topic. No looking. You will get things wrong. You will have gaps. That is the point — because finding those gaps IS the studying. The struggle to remember, even when you fail, is exactly what builds the memory.
>
> The research on this is overwhelming. Students who quiz themselves consistently outperform students who re-read, even when the re-readers spend more time studying. The method works. Most students just don't use it."

> **Cue:** You have 4–5 minutes. The push-up analogy is the turning point — land it clearly before moving to the mechanics. Do not add a second concept (spaced repetition, interleaving, etc.) — stay on retrieval practice.

> **Cue:** At around [6:30], check in briefly: "Any quick questions before we try it?" Take one, max. Redirect anything out of scope: "Great question — that's worth exploring separately. For now, let's do it."

**Transition:** "Now I want you to actually try it — right now."

---

### V — Verarbeitung [7:00–9:30]

**Purpose:** Participants do one complete retrieval practice attempt using their own course material. This is the ILO in action — they will leave having used the strategy, not just heard about it.

**The task:**
> Pick one topic you're currently studying or have an exam on soon. Close your eyes or flip your page over. Without looking at any notes or your phone, write down everything you can remember about that topic. You have 2 minutes.

> **Script:**
> "Here's what we're doing. You need a pen and a blank piece of paper — or the back of whatever you have. Pick one topic you're studying right now. Could be anything. A concept, a chapter, a term.
>
> In a moment I'm going to say go. When I do: close your notes, don't look at your phone, and write down everything you can remember about that topic. Don't worry about gaps. Don't worry about getting it perfect. Just write.
>
> Two minutes. Ready? Go."

> **Cue:** Start a visible timer — phone timer projected, countdown on screen, or say "Two minutes" and announce "30 seconds left" when you get there. While they work: walk quietly around the room. Don't hover. Don't talk.

> **Cue at 1:30:** "Thirty seconds — wrap up your thought."

**To close the task:**
> "Stop. Put your pen down. Now I want you to do one thing: look at what you wrote and notice what's NOT there. What couldn't you pull up? What's missing? Those gaps — right there — that is your actual study list. You just used retrieval practice."

**Transition:** "Last question before we finish."

---

### A — Assessing [9:30–10:00]

**Purpose:** Close the loop on the ILO. Check that participants have not just heard about retrieval practice, but actually experienced finding a gap.

**The question:**
> "Hands up — who just discovered at least one thing they thought they knew but couldn't actually recall?"

> **Script:**
> "Hands up — who just found at least one gap? Something you were surprised you couldn't remember?"
>
> *(Hands go up — most of them.)*
>
> "That feeling of finding a gap — that IS the strategy working. That discomfort is not failure. It's the learning happening. Next time you sit down to study: start there. Close your notes. Write what you remember. Use the gaps.
>
> That's retrieval practice. You've already done it once."

> **Cue:** If almost no hands go up, don't force it — say: "Even if you felt like you got most of it, try it tonight with a topic you haven't reviewed recently. The gaps show up faster than you expect." Then close.

---

## Contingency Notes

**If the group finishes Verarbeitung in under 1 minute:**
> Ask them to do a second topic: "If you feel like you covered that one, pick a second topic. Or go deeper on the same one — what else do you remember?"

**If the group is slow to start Verarbeitung (staring at blank page):**
> Prompt gently: "Any topic at all. What do you have an exam on next? Even if it's just one word — start there." Don't restart the timer; give the 30-second prompt earlier.

**If the Verarbeitung runs over (students still writing at 9:30):**
> Cut the close task cleanly: "Stop — I'll take the rest of the time." Move directly to the show-of-hands Assessing question. Skip the one-volunteer share.

**If a student asks about spaced repetition or other strategies during Informing:**
> "Yes — that pairs perfectly with this. That's the next level. For today, we're focused on just this one. Let's stay here."

**If the group is very experienced (e.g., grad students who already know about retrieval practice):**
> After the reactivation question: "Some of you may already use this. Great — then use the Verarbeitung to refine: try a topic that's genuinely difficult, and see how it goes." Adjust the Informing to be shorter and more confirmatory.
